newsitem.title: BRAZIL: COFFEE - Brazil council finally to be christened.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE - Brazil council finally to be christened.

text.p: Brazil's president is to attend a ceremony October 29 establishing the new council which will in future decide Brazilian coffee policy, with private sector officials hopeful of a swift start-up.
"I hope it will start meeting the next day," said Luis Suplicy Hafers, president of the Brazilian Rural Society and vice-president of the growers' National Coffee Council (CNC).
"This is a very big step forward to have coffee questions discussed and decided," he added.
Private sector representatives will attend the signing ceremony next week but even now it is still not clear what will be the actual make-up of the council to be known as the CDPC.

In the report drawn up by a parliamentary committee recommending the creation of a new council, it had been suggested it consist of up to 20 counsellors, split evenly between the private and public sectors, plus a president.
Within the private sector, the breakdown was seen as up to four producer representatives, and two each from exporters, roasters and the soluble coffee industry.
But in recent weeks there has been talk the total number of counsellors may be reduced to 12 and even to as low as 10.

This has caused concern particularly amongst exporters who have two groups - the Brazilian Coffee Exporters' Federation and the Brazilian Coffee Exporters' Association (Abecafe), leading to questions over who would act as representative, should there be only one place available.

Yesterday the president of Abecafe sent a letter to Industry and Commerce Minister Francisco Dornelles, widely expected to preside over the new council, expressing fears such a cut would endanger the council's representative nature.
"Any change to the composition recommended by the parliamentary committee would represent a return to zero after six months of debate and negotiation," Esteve said.
It "would cause an immediate deterioration in relations....and could compromise the representation and the legitimacy of the CDPC as well as render unviable its operation in the future," he added.

There has been no official communication however from the Industry and Commerce Ministry or elsewhere that the council may be downsized from the original proposal, said Maura Malta, executive secretary of the Soluble Industry Association.

Private sector officials are clearer about what should be the first tasks of the council, including discussing the postponement of some 250 million reais ($243 million) of producer debts, Hafers said.
Also the council is expected to decide on the funding of an official government crop forecast for 1997/98.
"I understand that the work has already been organised, however the council has to agree to pay for it," Hafers said.
